segments.title: Define what the research must explain
segments.body: A book project about a group of warships shows why a broad subject must be narrowed into answerable research needs. Strategic reasons for construction, tactical employment, operational use, recruitment patterns, and construction data each point toward different records. Researching why the ships were built and how they operated does not require the personal papers of every admiral who served aboard them. The plan may change when the first archive reveals another repository or line of enquiry, but an initial scope prevents indiscriminate collecting.

evidence.note: The talk distinguishes strategic, tactical, operational, personnel, and construction questions.

segments.summary: Start archival research by deciding whether the project needs strategic, tactical, operational, personnel, or construction evidence.

segments.title: Choose evidence for a story, fact, question, or theory
segments.body: The source type depends on whether the project seeks a personal story, a fact, an answer to a question, or evidence for a theory. Personal accounts and private papers often sit in specialist archives or libraries, while national facts may lead to government collections such as The National Archives. A narrow question can support a focused inquiry, but testing a theory calls for a wider evidential net. That distinction sets both the likely repositories and the scale of research.

evidence.note: Comparison of story and fact research, then narrow questions and theory testing.

segments.summary: A search for personal stories needs different collections from a factual inquiry, while testing a theory requires a wider net.

segments.title: Use a strong book to map the sources
segments.body: A Norman Friedman book about submarines in the two world wars shows how a strong academic work near the chosen subject can open an investigation. Its index and source list point to published Admiralty staff histories, technical histories, archive collections, and the repositories that hold them. References such as ADM series numbers can be carried directly into a catalogue search. Older bibliographies may call The National Archives the Public Record Office, or PRO, so recognising the former name helps recover their citations. Detailed notes make the earlier research route reproducible and turn secondary literature into a working map of the primary material.

evidence.note: The transcript demonstrates following Friedman and other academic bibliographies into Admiralty and archive sources.

segments.summary: A well-sourced scholarly book can lead researchers from its bibliography to staff histories, technical histories, and archive series.

segments.title: Follow journal citations to primary material
segments.body: The same source-tracing method works with JSTOR and other online scholarly journals. Article notes and citations can identify primary documents, collections, and the archives used by earlier researchers. Following those references shows which repositories and record series may matter before travel begins. A journal article can serve as both background reading and a route into the primary record.

evidence.note: The speaker recommends tracing journal citations to primary sources and archive lists.

segments.summary: Online journals provide another citation trail to the primary sources and repositories used by earlier researchers.

segments.title: Search catalogues broadly, then refine
segments.body: The demonstration starts with the term sloop, a 1920 to 1940 date range, and all participating archives in The National Archives' Discovery catalogue. The catalogue distinguishes records held by The National Archives from holdings reported by other UK repositories. Designs, hydrographic material, photographs, logbooks, correspondence, and unrelated hits show the breadth of a first search. The British Library, UK Hydrographic Office, Imperial War Museums, National Museums Liverpool, Hull History Centre, and local record offices all appear as possible destinations. Broad searching maps what survives and where it is held before the enquiry is narrowed.

evidence.note: A catalogue search for sloops illustrates date filters, other archives, and potentially relevant holdings.

segments.summary: A broad search for the term sloop can reveal National Archives records and holdings at other UK repositories.

segments.title: Read catalogue results for institutional clues
segments.body: Restricting the search to The National Archives and sorting by date exposes which departments created the records. Entries from the Admiralty, Colonial Office, Foreign Office, Treasury, and Board of Trade show that a naval question can cross diplomatic, colonial, financial, commercial, and labour policy. Treasury results include suspension of the 1928 cruiser programme and sloop construction proposed to relieve unemployment. Other entries concern minesweeping sloops for Australian training and a vessel loaned to the Australian Navy for surveying. Even a result that does not answer the main question can supply a department, date range, or record group for the next search.

evidence.note: Departmental origins, dates, and record groups in catalogue results provide clues for refining the next archival search.

segments.summary: Catalogue entries identify who created the records and supply departments, dates, and record groups for a more focused search.

segments.title: Plan document orders and archive visits
segments.body: Some catalogue records have not been digitised, leaving a visit or requested copy as the practical options. The demonstration distinguishes a standard visit with a smaller document allowance from a bulk order confined to one series. Booking limits and advance-order rules determine how much evidence can realistically be examined in a day or week. Counting records and checking their locations before travel turns a search list into a workable research schedule.

evidence.note: The speaker discusses non-digitised records, visits, bulk orders, and booking limits.

segments.summary: Once records are identified, account for digitisation limits, ordering rules, document caps, and the time needed for an archive visit.

segments.title: Contact smaller archives before travelling
segments.body: Smaller archives may rely heavily on volunteers, have incomplete online catalogues, or hold recent transfers from institutions that have closed. A courteous call or email should state the research topic and a known catalogue reference, then ask whether related material exists outside the online listing. Staff may identify uncatalogued deposits and explain local access arrangements. That exchange can show whether the visit needs one day or several and prevent a long trip built around an incomplete catalogue.

evidence.note: Contacting archives about material beyond their online listings and planning travel around the likely workload.

segments.summary: A polite enquiry can uncover uncatalogued or recently deposited material and prevent an under-planned research trip.

segments.title: Adapt the research cycle to access rules
segments.body: Advance booking replaced an earlier National Archives routine in which one day's findings guided the next document order. The old rhythm allowed important files to be read again at the following visit while a fresh group was brought out. Requiring documents and visits weeks ahead weakens that rapid feedback loop and shifts more work into pre-visit catalogue research. Archival method has to fit the repository's access system.

evidence.note: Advance-booking restrictions disrupted an earlier cycle of ordering, reading, and revisiting documents, requiring more catalogue work before an archive visit.

segments.summary: Advance booking and document limits can replace an iterative order-and-reread routine, so the research method must adjust to the archive's access system.

segments.title: Treat travel as part of the research budget
segments.body: An archive trip requires travel planning as well as a research plan. Estimate the document volume early enough to reserve consecutive days and avoid an expensive return journey. Examples from the Wirral, Newcastle, and Glasgow show that the nearest hotel may cost more or create a harder daily trip once equipment and transport are considered. Staff can offer candid local advice about where to stay. Early booking may make a week of research more practical than several short visits.

evidence.note: How document volume, repeat travel, accommodation location, and staff advice affect trip planning.

segments.summary: Document volume, transport, accommodation, and local advice determine whether a multi-day archive visit is affordable and productive.

segments.title: Pack for practical archive work
segments.body: Archive work needs a legible note-taking method, a capable camera, chargers, backup storage, cash, and a pencil. Some repositories lack adequate photocopying, so wide and close photographs may be the only practical way to capture a document. Reliable power and redundant storage protect a full day's work. Ink, food, and drink stay out of the reading room to protect original material. Older books may be inspected or excluded because people have tried to insert pages and falsify collections. The equipment plan must satisfy both preservation rules and the need to leave with a usable research record.

evidence.note: The final practical guidance covers equipment, backups, pencils, cameras, and reading-room restrictions.

segments.summary: Bring reliable note-taking and imaging equipment, backups, power, cash, and a pencil while respecting reading-room rules.
